title: Why Stainless Steel Resists Rust
text:
Ordinary steel is strong and cheap, but it has a serious weakness: when it is exposed to water and oxygen, it slowly turns into rust. Rust is a loose, flaky oxide that does not protect the metal underneath, so corrosion can continue until a part becomes too weak to use. For this reason, engineers have long searched for ways to keep steel from reacting with its environment.

One of the most successful answers is stainless steel. Its secret is chromium, which is added in amounts of at least about 10.5 percent. Chromium reacts with oxygen more readily than iron does and forms an extremely thin layer of chromium oxide on the surface. Unlike rust, this layer is dense and sticks firmly to the metal, so it acts as a barrier against further attack.

What makes the layer even more useful is that it can repair itself. If the surface is scratched, the exposed chromium quickly reacts with oxygen in the air, and the protective film forms again within a short time. However, stainless steel is not completely immune to damage. In environments rich in chloride, such as seawater or de-icing salt on roads, the film can break down locally, and small but deep pits may develop. For such conditions, grades containing molybdenum are usually preferred.

questions.q: The passage mainly explains ----.
options: why ordinary steel is still cheaper to produce and therefore more widely used than stainless steel
how an added element allows stainless steel to resist corrosion
the history of the invention of stainless steel
why seawater is the main cause of rust in all metals
how engineers in factories repair scratched steel surfaces by adding chromium to them afterwards
questions.explain: Metnin tamamı kromun oluşturduğu koruyucu oksit tabakasını anlatıyor. Tuzak: 'seawater' son paragrafta geçiyor ama ana fikir değil (kısmi bilgi).

questions.q: According to the passage, the chromium oxide layer differs from rust in that ----.
options: it is dense and adheres firmly to the metal
it forms more slowly than iron oxide
it is thick enough to be seen with the naked eye
it cannot form again once it has been damaged
it is completely resistant to chloride
questions.explain: 'Unlike rust, this layer is dense and sticks firmly to the metal' cümlesi dayanak. Tuzak: 'cannot form again' metnin tersi (kendini onarır).

questions.q: It can be inferred from the passage that stainless steel used in a marine environment ----.
options: never requires any kind of maintenance
contains less chromium than ordinary steel
will rust just as quickly as ordinary steel does once it is exposed to seawater and salt
gradually loses all of its chromium content and therefore needs replacing within a short time
may still be damaged locally unless an appropriate grade is selected
questions.explain: Klorürlü ortamda film yerel olarak bozulup çukur oluşabilir; molibdenli kaliteler tercih edilir. Tuzak: 'just as quickly as ordinary steel' aşırı genelleme; kromun tamamen kaybolması metinde yok.

title: Splitting Water for Clean Fuel
text:
Hydrogen is often described as the fuel of the future. When it is burned or used in a fuel cell, the only direct product is water, so it releases no carbon dioxide at the point of use. The problem is that pure hydrogen hardly exists on Earth. It is usually locked inside other compounds, and it must be separated before it can be used.

Today, most hydrogen is produced from natural gas in a process that releases large amounts of carbon dioxide. This kind of hydrogen is sometimes called grey hydrogen. A cleaner option is electrolysis, in which an electric current splits water into hydrogen and oxygen. If the electricity comes from wind or solar power, the result is known as green hydrogen.

Electrolysis is not a new idea; scientists demonstrated it more than two hundred years ago. What has changed is the falling cost of renewable electricity. Even so, green hydrogen remains more expensive than grey hydrogen, partly because electrolysers are costly and partly because some energy is lost in the conversion. Supporters argue that it will be most valuable in sectors that are difficult to electrify directly, such as steelmaking, fertiliser production and long-distance shipping.

questions.q: According to the passage, green hydrogen is different from grey hydrogen because ----.
options: it releases more energy when it is burned
it is extracted directly from natural deposits instead of being separated from other compounds
it is already cheaper to produce on a large scale than hydrogen made from natural gas
it produces carbon dioxide only in fuel cells
it is made by splitting water with power from renewable sources
questions.explain: 'If the electricity comes from wind or solar power, the result is known as green hydrogen.' Tuzak: 'cheaper' metnin tersi (hâlâ daha pahalı).

questions.q: The author mentions that electrolysis was demonstrated more than two hundred years ago in order to ----.
options: argue that the method is now outdated and should be replaced by newer technologies
show that the method itself is old and that cost is what has changed
explain why grey hydrogen is still widely used
prove that early scientists already relied on renewable energy sources in their experiments
criticise the slow progress of modern research
questions.explain: Yazarın amacı: 'not a new idea ... What has changed is the falling cost' — yöntem eski, değişen maliyet.

questions.q: It can be understood from the passage that supporters of green hydrogen ----.
options: believe that it should eventually replace electricity in all sectors, including households
deny that energy is lost during electrolysis
consider it already cheaper than hydrogen produced from natural gas in most industries
want to stop the production of fertilisers
regard it as particularly valuable where direct electrification is difficult
questions.explain: Son cümle: 'most valuable in sectors that are difficult to electrify directly'. Tuzak: 'all sectors' aşırı genelleme.

title: The Colour of the Sky
text:
Sunlight looks white, but it is actually a mixture of all the colours of the rainbow. Each colour corresponds to a different wavelength: red light has the longest waves in the visible range, while blue and violet light have the shortest. When sunlight enters the atmosphere, it meets countless gas molecules, mostly nitrogen and oxygen, which are much smaller than the wavelength of the light itself.

These tiny molecules scatter light in all directions, but they do not treat all colours equally. Short wavelengths are scattered far more strongly than long ones, an effect known as Rayleigh scattering after the British physicist who described it. As a result, blue light is spread across the whole sky, and wherever we look, some of it reaches our eyes.

If short wavelengths are scattered most, one might ask why the sky is not violet. There are several reasons. Part of the violet light is absorbed high in the atmosphere, sunlight contains slightly less violet than blue, and our eyes are more sensitive to blue. The same principle also explains red sunsets. When the Sun is low, its light travels through a much thicker layer of air, so most of the blue is scattered away before it reaches us, leaving mainly red and orange.

questions.q: The passage is mainly concerned with ----.
options: describing the chemical composition of the atmosphere
explaining why the sky appears blue and sunsets appear red
comparing how sensitive human eyes and animal eyes are to different colours of light
the life and work of a British physicist
showing that sunlight contains no violet light and is therefore not truly white
questions.explain: Metin Rayleigh saçılmasıyla mavi gökyüzünü ve kırmızı gün batımını açıklıyor. Tuzak: fizikçi sadece adı için anılıyor.

questions.q: According to the passage, the sky does not look violet partly because ----.
options: our eyes respond more strongly to blue than to violet
violet light has the longest wavelength
gas molecules in the atmosphere do not scatter violet light at all
sunlight contains no violet light
violet light travels faster than blue light and therefore leaves the atmosphere sooner
questions.explain: 'our eyes are more sensitive to blue' dayanak. Tuzak: 'contains no violet' — metin 'slightly less' diyor (kısmi doğru/çarpıtma).

questions.q: The word "it" in the sentence "some of it reaches our eyes" refers to ----.
options: the whole sky
Rayleigh scattering
blue light
the atmosphere
sunlight entering space
questions.explain: Önceki yan cümle 'blue light is spread across the whole sky' — 'it' mavi ışığa döner. Taktik: zamir en yakın uygun isme bakar, anlam kontrolü yap.

title: The Toughest Animals on Earth
text:
Tardigrades, also called water bears, are tiny animals usually less than a millimetre long. They live in many places, from mountain tops to the deep sea, but they are most often found in the thin films of water on moss and lichen. Under a microscope, they look like small, slow bears with eight legs, which explains their popular name.

What makes tardigrades famous is not their appearance but their ability to survive conditions that would kill almost any other animal. When their environment dries out, they pull in their legs, lose nearly all the water in their bodies and enter a state called cryptobiosis. In this state their metabolism almost stops. They can remain like this for years and then return to normal life within hours after water returns.

In laboratory tests, dried tardigrades have survived extreme cold, high levels of radiation and even a short period in the vacuum of space. Scientists believe that special proteins protect their cells by forming a glass-like material that holds delicate molecules in place. Researchers hope that understanding these proteins could one day help to store vaccines and other medicines without refrigeration. Nevertheless, active tardigrades are not indestructible, and many of them die when temperatures rise quickly.

questions.q: According to the passage, tardigrades enter cryptobiosis when ----.
options: they are exposed to the vacuum of space for years
the temperature rises quickly
they find water on moss and lichen
their environment dries out
they are placed under a microscope
questions.explain: 'When their environment dries out, they ... enter a state called cryptobiosis.' Tuzak: 'temperature rises quickly' son cümlede ölüm nedeni olarak geçiyor.

questions.q: Researchers are interested in tardigrade proteins mainly because they ----.
options: might help to store medicines without cooling
make the animals look like small, slow bears under a microscope
allow tardigrades to move faster
increase the animals' metabolism
are found only in animals living in the deep sea and on mountain tops
questions.explain: 'could one day help to store vaccines and other medicines without refrigeration'. refrigeration = cooling (eş anlam eşleştirme).

questions.q: It can be inferred from the last sentence that ----.
options: active tardigrades are far less resistant than dried ones
tardigrades cannot survive extreme cold, even when they are in a dried state
all tardigrades eventually die during laboratory tests involving radiation
cryptobiosis has no effect on survival
tardigrades prefer warm environments
questions.explain: Kuruyken uç koşullara dayanıyor, ama 'active tardigrades are not indestructible' — aktifken daha kırılgan. Tuzak: 'cannot survive extreme cold' metnin tersi.

title: When Corals Turn White
text:
Coral reefs cover a tiny fraction of the ocean floor, yet they support roughly a quarter of all marine species. A reef is built by small animals called coral polyps, which produce hard skeletons of calcium carbonate. Inside the tissues of most reef-building corals live microscopic algae. The algae carry out photosynthesis and share the sugars they make with the coral, which in turn provides them with shelter and nutrients.

This partnership is sensitive to temperature. When the water becomes only one or two degrees warmer than the usual summer maximum for several weeks, the relationship breaks down. The coral expels the algae, and because the algae give corals most of their colour, the white skeleton becomes visible through the transparent tissue. This process is known as bleaching.

A bleached coral is not dead, but it is starving and much more likely to catch diseases. If temperatures return to normal quickly, the algae can come back and the coral may recover. If the heat lasts too long, large areas of reef may die. Marine heatwaves have become more frequent as the oceans warm, and scientists warn that reefs now have less time to recover between bleaching events.

questions.q: According to the passage, a coral becomes white during bleaching because ----.
options: its calcium carbonate skeleton slowly changes into a different, whiter mineral
the algae produce too much sugar
it dies as soon as the water warms
it expels the algae responsible for most of its colour
diseases destroy the calcium carbonate skeleton and turn the tissue white
questions.explain: 'because the algae give corals most of their colour, the white skeleton becomes visible'. Tuzak: 'dies as soon as' — metin 'not dead' diyor.

questions.q: Which of the following is TRUE according to the passage?
options: A bleached coral may recover if the water cools down again quickly.
Coral reefs cover about a quarter of the ocean floor and support most marine species.
Algae provide corals with shelter and nutrients in return for the sugars they receive.
Bleaching occurs only when water becomes much colder.
Marine heatwaves have become rarer in recent years.
questions.explain: 'If temperatures return to normal quickly, the algae can come back and the coral may recover.' Tuzak: 'a quarter' türlerin oranı, alan değil; barınağı mercan veriyor.

questions.q: The author's main concern in the last paragraph is that ----.
options: bleached corals are always dead and can never be brought back to life by algae
scientists are still unable to measure ocean temperatures accurately during heatwaves
algae are harmful to coral reefs
reefs are getting less recovery time as heatwaves grow more common
corals should be moved to colder seas
questions.explain: Son cümle yazarın endişesini veriyor: 'less time to recover between bleaching events'.

title: Where Did the Moon Come From?
text:
For centuries, the origin of the Moon was a puzzle. Some scientists thought it had formed at the same time as Earth from the same cloud of material. Others suggested that Earth's gravity had captured a passing body, or that a fast-spinning young Earth had thrown off a piece of itself. Each idea, however, failed to explain at least one important observation.

The rock samples brought back by the Apollo missions changed the debate. They showed that lunar rocks are extremely similar to rocks from Earth's mantle in their chemical make-up, but the Moon has a much smaller iron core. They also suggested that the Moon's surface had once been covered by an ocean of molten rock.

Today, most researchers support the giant impact hypothesis. According to this idea, a planet-sized object, often called Theia, struck the young Earth about 4.5 billion years ago. The collision threw enormous amounts of hot material into orbit, and this material gradually came together to form the Moon. The model explains why the Moon is poor in iron and why it was once so hot. Even so, details remain under discussion, since computer simulations often predict that the Moon should contain more material from Theia than the samples appear to show.

questions.q: The main purpose of the passage is to ----.
options: explain how the Apollo missions were planned
argue that the Moon was captured by Earth's gravity rather than formed by a giant collision
show that computer simulations of the Moon's formation are now fully reliable and complete
trace changing views on the Moon's origin and identify the current favourite
compare the iron cores of all the planets
questions.explain: Metin eski hipotezlerden 'giant impact' görüşüne geçişi anlatıyor. Tuzak: 'captured' reddedilen fikirlerden biri.

questions.q: According to the passage, the Apollo samples showed that ----.
options: the Moon has a larger iron core than Earth, which explains why it was once so hot
the Moon's rocks resemble Earth's mantle in chemical composition
the Moon formed far away from Earth and was later pulled into orbit around it
Theia was made mostly of iron
the Moon has never been hot
questions.explain: 'lunar rocks are extremely similar to rocks from Earth's mantle in their chemical make-up'. Tuzak: çekirdek 'much smaller'.

questions.q: It can be understood from the last sentence that the giant impact hypothesis ----.
options: has been completely rejected by most scientists because of conflicting simulation results
is supported by no observations at all
explains every detail of the Moon's composition, including the amount of material from Theia
was proposed before the Apollo missions began
is widely accepted but still has unresolved problems
questions.explain: 'most researchers support' + 'details remain under discussion' = kabul görüyor ama sorunlu. 'Even so' zıtlık sinyali.

title: A Roll of Paper and a New Way of Listening
text:
Before the nineteenth century, a doctor who wanted to listen to a patient's heart or lungs had to press an ear directly against the patient's chest. This method, known as immediate auscultation, was uncomfortable for both people and often gave poor results, especially when the patient was overweight.

In 1816, the French physician René Laennec faced exactly this problem with a young female patient. Remembering that sound travels well through solid materials, he rolled a sheet of paper into a tube, placed one end on her chest and the other at his ear. To his surprise, he could hear the heartbeat far more clearly than ever before. Laennec soon replaced the paper with a hollow wooden cylinder and called his invention the stethoscope, from Greek words meaning "chest" and "to look at".

Laennec did more than build a tool. He spent years linking the sounds he heard to the diseases he later found in patients' bodies after death, and he published a detailed guide to these sounds. Over time, the design improved: flexible tubes and two earpieces were added, and modern versions can even record and amplify sounds electronically. Yet the basic idea of listening carefully to the body remains the same.

questions.q: According to the passage, Laennec first used a roll of paper because ----.
options: wooden cylinders were too expensive
he wanted to record and amplify the heartbeat electronically for later study
other doctors in France had already used paper tubes successfully for the same purpose
the patient had a lung disease
pressing his ear to the patient's chest was impractical
questions.explain: Doğrudan kulak dayamak rahatsız ve verimsizdi; genç kadın hastada 'exactly this problem'. Tuzak: elektronik kayıt modern dönem.

questions.q: The phrase "this problem" in the second paragraph refers to ----.
options: the high cost of the medical instruments that doctors needed in the early nineteenth century
the awkwardness of placing one's ear directly on the patient's chest
the lack of Greek names for new tools
the poor quality of paper in 1816
the failure of doctors to find the diseases they had heard in patients' bodies after death
questions.explain: 'This' önceki paragrafın tamamını (immediate auscultation zorluğu) özetler. Taktik: referans kelimesi geriye bakar.

questions.q: It can be inferred from the passage that Laennec's guide was valuable because it ----.
options: explained how to make paper tubes
described the history of Greek medicine
matched specific sounds with specific diseases
introduced electronic amplifiers that allowed doctors to hear quieter sounds more clearly
made physical examination of patients unnecessary, since doctors could rely on sounds alone
questions.explain: 'linking the sounds he heard to the diseases' — ses ile hastalığı eşleştiren rehber.

title: Robots That Learn by Trial and Error
text:
Traditional industrial robots are programmed step by step. An engineer tells the machine exactly where to move, how fast to go and when to close its gripper. This works very well in factories, where the same part arrives in the same position thousands of times a day. It works poorly, however, when objects vary in shape or the environment keeps changing.

Reinforcement learning offers a different approach. Instead of following fixed instructions, the robot tries an action and receives a numerical reward that tells it how well it did. Over many attempts, it gradually prefers actions that lead to higher rewards. In this way, a robot arm can learn to pick up unfamiliar objects or a walking robot can learn to keep its balance on rough ground.

The main difficulty is that learning requires a huge number of trials, and real robots are slow and can break. For this reason, researchers often train them first in computer simulations, where millions of attempts can be made in a few hours. The trained program is then transferred to the physical machine. Unfortunately, no simulation is perfect, so a robot that performs well on screen may still struggle in the real world, a problem that engineers call the reality gap.

questions.q: According to the passage, traditional programming of robots is most effective when ----.
options: objects frequently change their shape and the environment around the robot keeps changing
the same task is repeated in the same conditions
the robot is walking on rough ground
the robot receives a numerical reward telling it how well each movement was performed
simulations are not available
questions.explain: 'works very well in factories, where the same part arrives in the same position'.

questions.q: Researchers use computer simulations mainly because ----.
options: they are more realistic than the physical world and therefore give more reliable results
they make huge numbers of attempts possible quickly and safely
real robots cannot receive rewards
they completely remove the need for a physical robot once the program has been trained
simulated robots never make mistakes
questions.explain: Gerçek robot yavaş ve bozulabilir; simülasyonda 'millions of attempts ... in a few hours'. Tuzak: 'more realistic' — metin tersini söylüyor.

questions.q: The term "reality gap" describes ----.
options: the time needed to build a new robot
the physical gap between a robot's gripper and the object it is trying to pick up
how results on screen can differ from those in the real world
the difference in cost between traditional robots and those trained by trial and error
the distance a robot can walk without falling
questions.explain: Son cümle: ekranda iyi olan robot gerçekte zorlanabilir — buna 'reality gap' denir.

title: Cracks That Grow in Silence
text:
Most people imagine that a metal part breaks when it is loaded beyond its strength. In practice, a large share of mechanical failures happen at stresses well below that limit. The cause is fatigue: the gradual damage produced when a component is loaded and unloaded many times. Each cycle may seem harmless, but together they can initiate a microscopic crack, usually at a surface defect, a sharp corner or a hole where stress is concentrated.

Once a crack exists, every new cycle pushes it a tiny distance further. On the fracture surface, this slow growth often leaves curved lines called beach marks, which resemble the patterns left by waves on sand. Eventually, the remaining cross-section becomes too small to carry the load, and the part fails suddenly, often without visible warning.

The danger of fatigue became painfully clear in the 1950s, when several Comet jet airliners, the first of their kind, broke up in flight. Investigators found that cracks had started near openings in the pressurised fuselage, where repeated pressurisation cycles had concentrated stress. Since then, engineers have learned to round off corners, polish critical surfaces and introduce compressive stresses by shot peening. Equally important, they now design for inspection, calculating how fast a crack could grow so that it can be detected and repaired long before it becomes critical.

questions.q: The passage is mainly about ----.
options: the construction of the first jet airliners and the reasons why several of them broke up
why metals are stronger under compression
how fatigue cracks develop and how engineers reduce their danger
the methods engineers use to polish metal surfaces so that they look smooth and attractive
the patterns that waves leave on sand
questions.explain: Yorulma çatlağının başlaması, ilerlemesi ve önlemler anlatılıyor. Tuzak: Comet sadece örnek; 'beach marks' benzetme.

questions.q: According to the passage, fatigue cracks usually begin ----.
options: in the centre of thick, smooth parts
only when the load applied to the part exceeds the ultimate strength of the metal
after the part has already failed
on surfaces that have been shot peened, because the treatment introduces new defects
where stress builds up, for instance near holes or sharp corners
questions.explain: 'usually at a surface defect, a sharp corner or a hole where stress is concentrated'. Tuzak: 'exceeds the ultimate strength' metnin tersi (well below); shot peening koruyucu bir önlem.

questions.q: It can be inferred from the last sentence that modern design philosophy ----.
options: allows that cracks may form but aims to catch them in time
assumes that well-designed parts will never crack, so regular inspection is not required
relies only on stronger and more expensive materials to prevent fatigue from occurring
avoids inspecting parts in service
considers shot peening unnecessary
questions.explain: 'design for inspection ... detected and repaired long before it becomes critical' — çatlak olabilir, kritik olmadan bulunur (hasar toleransı).

title: Beyond Lithium
text:
Lithium-ion batteries power almost every phone and laptop, and they have made electric cars practical. Their success rests on lithium's light weight and its ability to store a large amount of energy in a small volume. Yet this success has raised concerns. Lithium deposits are concentrated in a few countries, mining can consume large volumes of water, and the price of lithium has swung dramatically in recent years.

Sodium-ion batteries are attracting attention as a possible alternative. Sodium is chemically similar to lithium, but it is far more abundant; it can be obtained from ordinary salt, which is found almost everywhere. Sodium-ion cells can also use aluminium instead of copper for one of their current collectors, which further reduces cost. In addition, some designs perform better than lithium-ion cells at low temperatures.

The main drawback is energy density. Sodium atoms are heavier and larger than lithium atoms, so a sodium-ion battery of the same weight stores less energy. This makes it less attractive for long-range cars, where every kilogram matters. However, many applications do not demand the highest energy density. For storing solar power in stationary systems or for small urban vehicles, low cost and safety may matter more than weight. For this reason, experts generally see sodium-ion technology not as a replacement for lithium-ion batteries but as a complement to them.

questions.q: According to the passage, one advantage of sodium is that it ----.
options: is lighter than lithium and therefore allows batteries to store more energy
stores more energy per kilogram than lithium
is widely available and inexpensive to obtain
requires copper current collectors
is found in only a few countries, which keeps its price stable
questions.explain: 'far more abundant; it can be obtained from ordinary salt'. Tuzak: 'lighter' ve 'more energy' metnin tersi.

questions.q: Sodium-ion batteries are less suitable for long-range cars because ----.
options: they cannot operate at low temperatures
they are more expensive to produce than lithium-ion batteries of similar size
they require large amounts of water
they store less energy for the same weight
they are less safe than lithium-ion batteries when used at very high speeds
questions.explain: 'a sodium-ion battery of the same weight stores less energy' + 'where every kilogram matters'.

questions.q: The author's view of sodium-ion technology can best be described as ----.
options: highly critical, rejecting it as impractical because of its low energy density
enthusiastic, claiming that it will soon replace lithium-ion batteries completely
indifferent, showing no interest in its future
balanced, viewing it as a complement rather than a substitute
confused, giving contradictory information about it
questions.explain: Yazar avantaj ve dezavantajı veriyor; son cümle 'not as a replacement ... but as a complement'. Ton: dengeli/objektif.

title: Bread from Air
text:
Nitrogen makes up about 78 percent of the air, yet plants cannot use it in that form. The two atoms in a nitrogen molecule are held together by a triple bond, one of the strongest bonds in chemistry. Before crops can absorb nitrogen, it must be "fixed", that is, converted into compounds such as ammonia or nitrates. In nature, this is done mainly by certain bacteria and, to a small extent, by lightning.

At the beginning of the twentieth century, farmers relied on natural fertilisers, and scientists warned that the world's supply would soon fail to keep pace with a growing population. The German chemist Fritz Haber found a solution in 1909. He showed that nitrogen and hydrogen could be combined into ammonia at high pressure and a moderately high temperature in the presence of an iron-based catalyst. Carl Bosch, an engineer at the company BASF, then faced the enormous task of turning a laboratory experiment into an industrial process, which required new steels able to withstand hydrogen at high pressure.

The Haber-Bosch process is often said to support the food supply of roughly half of humanity. Its benefits, however, come at a price. The process consumes a significant share of the world's energy, and most of the hydrogen it uses is still made from fossil fuels. Moreover, excess fertiliser washes into rivers and seas, where it can cause harmful algal blooms.

questions.q: According to the passage, plants cannot use atmospheric nitrogen directly because ----.
options: it makes up only a small part of the air and is therefore too scarce to absorb
its atoms are held together by a very strong bond
lightning destroys most of it
it is already a compound of ammonia and nitrates that plants cannot break down
bacteria consume all of it
questions.explain: 'triple bond, one of the strongest bonds' — önce 'fix' edilmesi gerekir. Tuzak: '78 percent' büyük oran.

questions.q: It can be understood from the passage that Carl Bosch's contribution was ----.
options: discovering that bacteria fix nitrogen
inventing the iron-based catalyst that allowed nitrogen and hydrogen to combine in 1909
warning about the shortage of natural fertilisers
reducing the large amount of energy the process consumed by using new types of steel
scaling up Haber's method so that it could run in factories
questions.explain: 'turning a laboratory experiment into an industrial process'. Tuzak: 1909 ve katalizör Haber'e ait.

questions.q: The last paragraph mainly points out that the Haber-Bosch process ----.
options: no longer plays a role in food production
now uses mainly renewable hydrogen instead of hydrogen made from fossil fuels
has great benefits but also serious environmental costs
has solved the problem of algal blooms
supports the food supply of all humanity without causing any environmental problems
questions.explain: 'Its benefits, however, come at a price' — enerji, fosil yakıt, alg patlaması. Tuzak: 'all humanity' — metin 'roughly half'.

title: Molecular Scissors
text:
For decades, changing a specific gene in a living organism was slow, expensive and unreliable. That situation changed dramatically after 2012, when researchers showed that a bacterial defence system known as CRISPR could be turned into a precise tool for editing DNA.

In bacteria, CRISPR acts as a kind of immune memory. When a virus attacks, the bacterium stores a short piece of the virus's DNA in its own genome. If the same virus returns, the bacterium produces an RNA copy of the stored piece, which guides a protein called Cas9 to the matching viral DNA. Cas9 then cuts the DNA and disables the invader. Scientists realised that by designing their own guide RNA, they could direct Cas9 to almost any sequence in almost any organism. Once the DNA is cut, the cell's repair machinery takes over, and researchers can exploit this process to disable a gene or insert a new one.

The technique has spread to laboratories around the world because it is cheap and relatively easy to use. It is already being applied to crops, to animal models of disease and, in clinical trials, to inherited blood disorders such as sickle cell disease. Nevertheless, CRISPR is not flawless. Cas9 sometimes cuts at unintended sites, and changes made to embryos would be passed on to future generations, which raises ethical questions that science alone cannot answer.

questions.q: According to the passage, in bacteria CRISPR functions as ----.
options: a method of producing new proteins for growth
a way of passing genes to future generations
a repair system for damaged cells
a defence system that remembers viruses
a laboratory tool designed by scientists
questions.explain: 'In bacteria, CRISPR acts as a kind of immune memory'. Tuzak: 'laboratory tool' — bilim insanlarının sonradan dönüştürdüğü hâli.

questions.q: The phrase "this process" in the second paragraph refers to ----.
options: the storage of viral DNA in bacteria
the attack of a virus on a bacterium
the repair of cut DNA by the cell
the design of guide RNA by researchers
the spread of CRISPR to laboratories
questions.explain: Hemen önceki ifade: 'the cell's repair machinery takes over' — 'this process' hücrenin onarımıdır.

questions.q: It can be inferred from the last paragraph that the author believes ----.
options: choices about altering embryos are not purely a matter for science
CRISPR should be banned in all laboratories until the problem of unintended cuts is solved
unintended cuts never occur with Cas9
the ethical questions raised by editing embryos have already been fully resolved by scientists
sickle cell disease cannot be treated with CRISPR
questions.explain: 'ethical questions that science alone cannot answer'. Tuzak: 'banned' metinde yok (aşırı yorum).

title: The Thawing North
text:
Across large parts of Siberia, Alaska and northern Canada, the ground beneath the surface has remained frozen for thousands of years. This permanently frozen soil, called permafrost, contains the remains of plants and animals that never fully decomposed because microbes cannot work in such cold conditions. Scientists estimate that permafrost holds roughly twice as much carbon as the atmosphere currently does.

As the Arctic warms faster than the global average, this frozen store is beginning to thaw. When it does, microbes become active again and break down the old organic matter, releasing carbon dioxide and, in waterlogged soils, methane, a gas that traps far more heat over a short period. These emissions add to warming, which in turn causes more thawing. Climate scientists call such self-reinforcing processes positive feedbacks, although there is nothing positive about their consequences.

Thawing also creates problems on the surface. Roads, pipelines and buildings designed for solid frozen ground can crack or sink as the soil softens. In some regions, coastlines are collapsing into the sea at alarming rates. The pace of future emissions is still uncertain, partly because plants may grow more vigorously in a warmer Arctic and absorb some of the released carbon. However, most studies suggest that this uptake will not be large enough to offset the losses.

questions.q: According to the passage, organic matter in permafrost has not fully decomposed because ----.
options: it contains no carbon
plants absorb all of it
the cold prevents microbes from breaking it down
methane trapped in the frozen soil prevents microbes from becoming active
it is buried deep under the sea where no oxygen can reach the remains
questions.explain: 'never fully decomposed because microbes cannot work in such cold conditions'.

questions.q: The author uses the phrase "there is nothing positive about their consequences" in order to ----.
options: criticise climate scientists for using wrong data when they describe Arctic emissions
make clear that the technical term does not imply good effects
suggest that such feedbacks will eventually slow down warming in the Arctic region
show that methane is harmless
argue that the Arctic is not warming
questions.explain: 'positive feedback' terimi 'kendini besleyen' anlamında; yazar 'iyi' anlamına gelmediğini vurguluyor (yazarın amacı).

questions.q: It can be concluded from the last paragraph that increased plant growth in the Arctic ----.
options: will completely stop future emissions by absorbing all of the carbon released
is the main cause of the coastal collapse and the damage to roads and pipelines
has made permafrost refreeze
will damage roads and pipelines
is unlikely to fully compensate for carbon released by thawing
questions.explain: 'this uptake will not be large enough to offset the losses'. offset = compensate (eş anlam).

title: Shadows of Distant Worlds
text:
Until the 1990s, no planet had been confirmed around a star like our Sun. Today, astronomers have catalogued more than five thousand such worlds, known as exoplanets. Most of them have never been seen directly, because a planet is extremely faint compared with the star it orbits. Instead, they are detected by the effects they have on their stars.

The most productive technique is the transit method. If a planet's orbit happens to be aligned with our line of sight, the planet passes in front of its star once every orbit and blocks a small fraction of its light. A telescope that monitors the star's brightness records a tiny, regular dip. The depth of the dip reveals the size of the planet relative to the star, while the time between dips gives the length of its year. Space telescopes such as Kepler and TESS have used this approach to discover thousands of candidates.

The method has limitations. Only planets with suitably aligned orbits can be detected, and a single dip may be caused by a passing object or by spots on the star itself. Therefore, astronomers usually require several transits and confirmation by another technique before they accept a discovery. When it works, however, the transit method can offer even more: as starlight passes through a planet's atmosphere during a transit, it carries chemical fingerprints that reveal which gases are present.

questions.q: According to the passage, most exoplanets have not been observed directly because ----.
options: they are very dim compared with their host stars
they are too close to Earth
their orbits are never aligned with our line of sight
telescopes cannot measure brightness
they have no atmospheres
questions.explain: 'a planet is extremely faint compared with the star it orbits'. faint = dim.

questions.q: According to the passage, the time between two dips in brightness indicates ----.
options: the size of the planet
how long the planet takes to orbit its star
which gases are present in the planet's atmosphere during a transit
the distance between the star and Earth, measured in light-years
the number of spots on the star
questions.explain: 'the time between dips gives the length of its year'. Tuzak: dip derinliği boyutu verir.

questions.q: Astronomers require several transits before accepting a discovery mainly because ----.
options: planets never pass in front of the same star twice in a single year
Kepler and TESS cannot record dips
a single dip might have another cause
atmospheres block all starlight
the transit method is the least productive of all the techniques astronomers use
questions.explain: 'a single dip may be caused by a passing object or by spots ... Therefore ...' — neden-sonuç bağlacı.

title: Seconds Before the Shaking
text:
Despite more than a century of research, scientists still cannot predict earthquakes. No reliable signal has been found that tells us, days or hours in advance, exactly where and when a major rupture will occur. What seismologists can do is estimate long-term probabilities: they can say, for example, that a particular fault has a high chance of producing a large earthquake within the next few decades.

A more modest but practical goal is early warning. An earthquake releases different kinds of waves. The first to arrive are primary or P-waves, which travel fast but usually cause little damage. They are followed by slower secondary or S-waves and surface waves, which produce most of the destructive shaking. Because electronic signals travel far faster than seismic waves, a network of sensors near the fault can detect the P-waves, estimate the size and location of the earthquake within seconds, and send an alert to areas further away before the strong shaking arrives.

The warning time is short, ranging from a few seconds to perhaps a minute, and places very close to the epicentre may receive no warning at all. Even so, a few seconds can be enough for trains to slow down, surgeons to stop operations and people to take cover under a table. Systems of this kind already operate in Japan, Mexico and parts of the United States.

options: tells people days or even hours in advance exactly when an earthquake will occur
picks up a quake already in progress and warns places farther away
is based on long-term probabilities that are calculated separately for each fault
works only very close to the epicentre
prevents surface waves from forming
questions.explain: Erken uyarı başlamış depremin P-dalgasını yakalayıp uzak bölgelere haber verir. Tuzak: 'days or even hours in advance' tahmin (prediction) tanımı ve mümkün değil; uzun vadeli olasılık da tahminle ilgili.

options: P-waves cause the most damage
S-waves arrive before P-waves
sensors near the fault can predict earthquakes several days before they begin

questions.explain: 'Because electronic signals travel far faster than seismic waves' — 'because' doğrudan dayanak.

questions.q: It can be inferred from the passage that people living very near the epicentre ----.
options: receive the longest warning time because the sensors are located closest to them
feel only P-waves

questions.explain: 'places very close to the epicentre may receive no warning at all'. Tuzak: 'longest warning' tersi.

title: Electricity Without Resistance
text:
When an electric current flows through an ordinary wire, the moving electrons collide with the vibrating atoms of the metal and lose energy as heat. This resistance is why cables become warm and why a portion of electricity is lost on its way from power stations to homes. In 1911, however, the Dutch physicist Heike Kamerlingh Onnes discovered something remarkable. When he cooled mercury to about four degrees above absolute zero, its electrical resistance suddenly disappeared.

This phenomenon, called superconductivity, has two striking features. First, a current started in a superconducting loop can continue to flow for years without any power source. Second, a superconductor pushes magnetic fields out of its interior, which allows a magnet to float above it. Explaining these effects took almost fifty years; the accepted theory states that, at very low temperatures, electrons form pairs that move through the material without scattering.

Superconductors are already essential in hospital MRI scanners and particle accelerators, where they create powerful magnetic fields. Their wider use, however, is limited by the need for extreme cooling, which is expensive and complex. In 1986, researchers discovered ceramic materials that become superconducting at much higher temperatures, though still far below room temperature. Since then, the search for a superconductor that works under everyday conditions has continued, and several widely publicised claims have failed to survive independent testing.

options: magnetic fields are pushed out of the wire's interior as the current flows through it
electrons form pairs at low temperatures and move without scattering through the metal
electrons collide with vibrating atoms and produce heat
the wire is cooled below absolute zero
currents continue to flow for years
questions.explain: İlk cümle: elektronlar titreşen atomlara çarpar, ısı olarak enerji kaybolur.

questions.q: According to the passage, the wider use of superconductors is limited because ----.
options: they require extreme cooling, which is expensive and complex
the ceramic materials discovered in 1986 work only at room temperature
currents in superconducting loops stop flowing after a few years
they cannot create magnetic fields strong enough for MRI scanners
their electrons collide with vibrating atoms and lose energy as heat

title: Instructions Instead of Ingredients
text:
Traditional vaccines usually expose the immune system to a weakened or inactivated virus, or to a purified piece of it. Producing these ingredients can take months, because the virus or its proteins must be grown in eggs or cell cultures. Messenger RNA vaccines follow a different strategy. Rather than delivering the viral protein itself, they deliver genetic instructions that allow the body's own cells to make a harmless piece of that protein for a short time.

The idea is decades old, but early attempts faced serious obstacles. Injected RNA was quickly destroyed and could trigger strong inflammation. Two advances solved much of the problem. Researchers found that slightly modifying the building blocks of RNA made it far less likely to provoke an unwanted immune reaction, and they developed tiny fat particles, called lipid nanoparticles, that protect the RNA and help it enter cells.

When the COVID-19 pandemic began, these advances allowed vaccines to be designed within days of the virus's genetic sequence being published. Because the platform remains the same and only the instructions change, mRNA vaccines can in principle be updated quickly when a virus mutates. They are not without drawbacks: some formulations must be stored at very low temperatures, which complicates distribution in regions with poor infrastructure. Nevertheless, researchers are now testing the approach against influenza and even certain cancers.

options: contain a weakened or inactivated form of the whole virus grown in eggs
are grown in eggs for several months
do not involve the immune system
can be stored easily at room temperature and distributed without special equipment
make the body's own cells produce part of a viral protein
questions.explain: 'deliver genetic instructions that allow the body's own cells to make a harmless piece of that protein'.

questions.q: The two advances mentioned in the second paragraph were important because they ----.
options: made RNA more stable and less likely to cause inflammation
allowed vaccines to be grown in cell cultures
removed the need for any delivery system
made the vaccines considerably cheaper to produce than traditional ones grown in eggs
reduced the time needed to publish the genetic sequence of a newly discovered virus
questions.explain: Değiştirilmiş yapı taşları istenmeyen bağışıklık tepkisini azaltır, lipid nanopartiküller RNA'yı korur.

options: cannot be updated quickly when a virus mutates because the platform must be redesigned
take years to design
are effective only against cancer

questions.explain: 'must be stored at very low temperatures, which complicates distribution'. Tuzak: 'cannot be updated' tersi.

title: Air Through Molten Iron
text:
In the early nineteenth century, iron was produced in two main forms. Cast iron, made in blast furnaces, contained a lot of carbon; it was cheap and easy to shape but brittle. Wrought iron contained very little carbon and was tough, yet it had to be produced by hand in small batches through a laborious process called puddling. Steel, with an intermediate carbon content, combined strength and toughness, but it was so expensive that it was used mainly for tools, springs and weapons.

In 1856, the English inventor Henry Bessemer announced a method that changed this situation. He blew air through molten pig iron in a large vessel known as a converter. The oxygen in the air reacted with carbon and silicon in the metal, and these reactions released so much heat that the iron stayed liquid without any additional fuel. In about twenty minutes, several tonnes of iron could be converted into steel.

The process was not an immediate success. Early Bessemer steel was often brittle, because the method did not remove phosphorus and left too much oxygen in the metal. The problems were solved by others: adding manganese improved quality, and in the late 1870s Sidney Gilchrist Thomas introduced a basic lining that captured phosphorus. With cheap steel available, railways, ships and skyscrapers could be built on a new scale. The Bessemer converter has long disappeared, but its central idea survives in modern oxygen steelmaking.

options: it was more brittle than cast iron
it contained no carbon
it could be produced only in blast furnaces, which were rare at the time
it was too costly for large-scale use
it was weaker than wrought iron and could not be used for railways
questions.explain: 'it was so expensive that it was used mainly for tools, springs and weapons' (so...that = sonuç).

options: the converter was heated by electricity supplied from an external source
pig iron melts at room temperature
the chemical reactions inside the vessel released sufficient heat

the whole process took only about twenty minutes, so the metal had no time to cool
questions.explain: 'these reactions released so much heat that the iron stayed liquid without any additional fuel'.

options: claim that he invented the converter several years before Bessemer announced his method
argue that phosphorus, when captured by a basic lining, actually improves steel quality

suggest that Bessemer's idea was useless
questions.explain: Paragrafın mantığı: 'not an immediate success ... The problems were solved by others'. Thomas fosforu tutan astarı getirdi.

title: Cleaning the Exhaust
text:
A petrol engine does not burn its fuel perfectly. Along with carbon dioxide and water, its exhaust contains carbon monoxide, unburnt hydrocarbons and nitrogen oxides, all of which harm human health and contribute to smog. Since the 1970s, stricter air-quality laws in many countries have made it necessary to remove most of these pollutants before they leave the tailpipe.

The device that does this is the catalytic converter. Inside a metal case is a ceramic block with thousands of narrow channels, which give it an enormous surface area. The walls of these channels are coated with tiny amounts of precious metals, mainly platinum, palladium and rhodium. These metals act as catalysts: they speed up chemical reactions without being consumed themselves. Carbon monoxide and hydrocarbons are oxidised to carbon dioxide and water, while nitrogen oxides are reduced to harmless nitrogen.

For all three reactions to work efficiently at once, the engine must run with a very precise ratio of air to fuel. An oxygen sensor in the exhaust continuously sends information to the engine's computer, which adjusts the fuel supply many times per second. The converter also works poorly until it is hot, so a large share of emissions from a modern car occur in the first minutes after a cold start. Because the precious metals are valuable, catalytic converters have unfortunately become a frequent target of thieves.

options: are consumed after each journey
convert carbon dioxide back into carbon monoxide and unburnt hydrocarbons
accelerate reactions without being used up
cool the exhaust gases
replace the need for an oxygen sensor and an engine computer in modern cars
questions.explain: 'they speed up chemical reactions without being consumed themselves'. speed up = accelerate; consumed = used up.

questions.q: The oxygen sensor mentioned in the passage is needed in order to ----.
options: measure how much platinum and palladium remain in the converter after each trip
heat the converter quickly after a cold start so that it begins to work sooner
detect thieves
help keep the air-to-fuel ratio within a narrow range
increase the production of nitrogen oxides
questions.explain: Sensör bilgi gönderir, bilgisayar yakıtı ayarlar — 'very precise ratio of air to fuel'.

questions.q: It can be inferred from the passage that short car trips from a cold start ----.
options: produce no pollutants at all, since the engine has not yet reached full power
make the converter work most efficiently because the engine is still cool
produce relatively high emissions per kilometre

require no fuel adjustment
questions.explain: Konvertör ısınana kadar kötü çalışır; emisyonun büyük kısmı ilk dakikalarda. Kısa yolculukta oran yüksek olur (çıkarım).

title: Forecasting with Machines
text:
For more than half a century, weather forecasts have been produced by numerical models. These programs divide the atmosphere into millions of boxes and solve the physical equations of fluid motion, heat and moisture for each one. They are remarkably skilful, but they require some of the most powerful supercomputers in the world, and a single global forecast can take hours of computing time.

In the past few years, a different approach has emerged. Technology companies and research centres have trained machine-learning models on decades of past weather data. Instead of solving physical equations, these models learn statistical patterns that link the state of the atmosphere at one moment to its state a few hours later. Once trained, they can produce a ten-day global forecast in about a minute on a single processor, and in several tests their accuracy has matched or exceeded that of leading traditional models for many variables.

Meteorologists, however, are not ready to abandon physics. Machine-learning models are trained on data that were themselves created with the help of traditional models, so they still depend on them. They may also perform poorly for rare and extreme events, which by definition appear infrequently in the training data. Many experts therefore expect a hybrid future, in which physical models and machine learning work together, each compensating for the other's weaknesses.

options: solve the physical equations of fluid motion more precisely than traditional models do
do not require any past data
always predict extreme events accurately
have already replaced traditional models completely in most weather centres
take far less time and far less computing power to produce
questions.explain: 'ten-day global forecast in about a minute on a single processor'. Tuzak: 'replaced traditional models completely' metnin tersi (hibrit gelecek bekleniyor).

questions.q: Meteorologists are reluctant to abandon physical models partly because ----.
options: physical models are cheaper to run
machine-learning models are never accurate for ordinary variables such as temperature
rare and extreme events appear far too frequently in the data used for training

questions.explain: 'trained on data that were themselves created with the help of traditional models'.

options: rely only on machine learning once enough past data has been collected
return to forecasts made without computers

questions.explain: 'Many experts therefore expect a hybrid future'.

title: The Smallest Atom, the Biggest Threat
text:
High-strength steels have allowed engineers to build lighter bridges, safer cars and deeper offshore wells. Paradoxically, the stronger a steel is, the more vulnerable it tends to be to one of the smallest of all intruders: hydrogen. Because hydrogen atoms are tiny, they can diffuse into the crystal lattice of steel even at room temperature. Sources are surprisingly common, ranging from corrosion reactions and acid pickling to welding with damp electrodes and electroplating.

Once inside, hydrogen atoms tend to accumulate at regions of high stress, such as the tip of a small crack or a notch. There they weaken the bonds between iron atoms and promote cracking at loads that the material would normally carry without difficulty. The resulting failure, known as hydrogen embrittlement, is particularly treacherous because it is often delayed. A bolt may be tightened without any sign of trouble and then fracture hours or even weeks later, after enough hydrogen has migrated to the critical spot.

Although the phenomenon has been studied for more than a century, its exact mechanism is still debated, and several competing theories may each describe part of the truth. In practice, engineers rely on a combination of measures: limiting the hardness of components exposed to hydrogen, baking parts after electroplating so that absorbed hydrogen can escape, and designing microstructures containing fine particles that trap hydrogen harmlessly. The issue is gaining new urgency. If hydrogen is to be transported through existing gas pipelines or stored at high pressure in steel tanks, the compatibility of these materials with hydrogen will have to be demonstrated rather than assumed.

options: completely prevents hydrogen from entering the lattice
makes delayed failures impossible
has no connection with the problem
is achieved mainly by adding hydrogen
generally increases the risk rather than reducing it
questions.explain: 'Paradoxically, the stronger a steel is, the more vulnerable it tends to be' — the more..., the more... karşılaştırma yapısı.

options: failure may occur long after a component has been loaded
it can be detected only at very high temperatures after the part has been baked

questions.explain: 'often delayed ... fracture hours or even weeks later'. treacherous = sinsi. Tuzak: 'visible deformation' tersi.

options: the mechanism of embrittlement has finally been fully explained by a single accepted theory

title: Making Steel Without Coal
text:
Steel is indispensable to modern life, but its production is responsible for roughly seven to nine percent of global carbon dioxide emissions. Most of these emissions arise in the blast furnace, where coke made from coal serves both as a fuel and as the agent that removes oxygen from iron ore. Because this chemical role cannot be performed by electricity alone, decarbonising steel is widely regarded as one of the hardest challenges of the energy transition.

One promising route replaces carbon with hydrogen. In direct reduction, iron ore pellets react with a hot reducing gas in a shaft furnace below the melting point of iron, producing a porous solid known as direct reduced iron, or sponge iron. Plants of this type already operate in regions with cheap natural gas, which supplies a mixture of hydrogen and carbon monoxide. If the gas is pure hydrogen produced with renewable electricity, the main by-product becomes water vapour instead of carbon dioxide. The sponge iron is then usually melted in an electric arc furnace.

The obstacles are considerable. Producing enough green hydrogen for a single large steelworks would require vast amounts of renewable electricity. Direct reduction also works best with high-grade ore containing few impurities, and such ore is in limited supply. Furthermore, existing blast furnaces represent enormous investments that companies are reluctant to abandon before the end of their working lives. For these reasons, many producers are pursuing transitional strategies, for instance injecting hydrogen into existing furnaces or capturing carbon dioxide, while pilot plants test whether fully hydrogen-based steelmaking can operate reliably on an industrial scale.

options: steel production accounts for most of the world's carbon dioxide emissions from industry

hydrogen reacts too slowly with ore
coal is needed chemically to strip oxygen from the ore, not merely as fuel
iron ore contains no oxygen

options: is made in a blast furnace in which coke removes oxygen from the iron ore

options: Most of them have already closed their blast furnaces and switched to direct reduction.

title: A Star in a Bottle
text:
The Sun shines because, in its core, hydrogen nuclei fuse into helium and release enormous amounts of energy. Reproducing this process on Earth has been a goal of physicists since the 1950s. Fusion fuel is abundant, the reactions produce no carbon dioxide, and, unlike fission reactors, a fusion plant would not generate long-lived radioactive waste in large quantities or be at risk of a runaway chain reaction.

The difficulty lies in the conditions required. Atomic nuclei are positively charged and repel each other, so they must collide at extremely high speeds, which means heating the fuel to temperatures of the order of a hundred million degrees. At such temperatures, matter becomes a plasma that would destroy any container it touched. The most developed approach, the tokamak, holds the plasma in a doughnut-shaped chamber using powerful magnetic fields. An alternative, inertial confinement, fires intense lasers at a tiny fuel pellet to compress and heat it in a fraction of a second.

In December 2022, the National Ignition Facility in the United States reported that a laser experiment had released more fusion energy than the laser light delivered to the target. The achievement was widely celebrated as a historic milestone. Yet it must be interpreted with care: the lasers themselves consumed far more electricity than the fusion reaction produced, and a power plant would need to repeat such reactions many times per second. Meanwhile, the international ITER tokamak under construction in France has faced repeated delays and rising costs. Fusion, critics joke, has always been thirty years away; its supporters reply that the joke is finally becoming outdated.

options: plasma cools down too quickly when it is held inside powerful magnetic fields
fusion would otherwise produce large amounts of long-lived radioactive waste
lasers cannot operate at low temperatures
like charges make nuclei repel, so they must meet at high speed
hydrogen turns into helium only in the Sun
questions.explain: 'nuclei are positively charged and repel each other, so they must collide at extremely high speeds, which means heating...'.

options: the experiment was never repeated
the lasers drew far more electricity than the reaction released
the laser light delivered almost no energy to the fuel target during the experiment

the reaction produced carbon dioxide
questions.explain: 'the lasers themselves consumed far more electricity than the fusion reaction produced'. Hedefe giden ışık enerjisi < füzyon, ama toplam elektrik >> füzyon.

questions.q: The tone of the final sentence can best be described as ----.
options: cautiously hopeful, while acknowledging past scepticism

questions.explain: Eleştirmenlerin şakası (hep 30 yıl uzakta) aktarılıyor, destekçiler şakanın eskidiğini söylüyor — temkinli umut.

title: Fragile Qubits
text:
Ordinary computers process information in bits, each of which is either a zero or a one. Quantum computers use qubits, which can exist in a superposition of both states at once. When several qubits become entangled, their states are linked in such a way that describing one of them independently of the others is no longer possible. In principle, these properties allow a quantum computer to explore certain problems in ways that no classical machine could match, such as simulating complex molecules or factoring very large numbers.

The same features that make qubits powerful also make them extraordinarily fragile. Any unwanted interaction with the environment, whether a stray vibration, a fluctuation in temperature or a passing electromagnetic signal, can disturb the delicate quantum state. This process, known as decoherence, causes the qubit to lose its information, often within a fraction of a second. For this reason, many leading devices operate inside refrigerators cooled to a few thousandths of a degree above absolute zero and are carefully shielded from outside disturbances.

Even with such precautions, errors are unavoidable. The proposed solution is quantum error correction, in which the information of one reliable "logical" qubit is spread across many physical qubits, so that errors can be detected and fixed without directly measuring, and thereby destroying, the stored information. The cost is steep: estimates suggest that a single logical qubit might require hundreds or even thousands of physical ones. Recent experiments have shown that adding more physical qubits can indeed reduce the error rate, a crucial proof of principle. Nevertheless, the large, fault-tolerant machines needed for the most valuable applications remain, by most estimates, years away.

questions.q: According to the passage, decoherence ----.
options: is the process by which several qubits become entangled with one another
results from undesired contact between qubits and their surroundings
improves the stability of logical qubits by spreading their information widely
takes place only in classical computers
occurs only at room temperature
questions.explain: 'Any unwanted interaction with the environment ... This process, known as decoherence'.

title: Beyond the Genetic Code
text:
Almost every cell in your body contains the same DNA, yet a nerve cell and a liver cell look and behave very differently. The explanation lies not in the genes themselves but in which genes are switched on or off. The study of such heritable changes in gene activity that do not involve alterations to the DNA sequence is called epigenetics.

One of the best-understood mechanisms is DNA methylation, in which small chemical tags called methyl groups are attached to the DNA, usually silencing nearby genes. Another involves the proteins called histones, around which DNA is wound. Chemical modifications to histones can loosen or tighten this packaging, making genes more or less accessible to the machinery that reads them. These patterns are copied when cells divide, which is why a skin cell gives rise to more skin cells rather than to neurons.

What has attracted public interest is evidence that the environment can influence these marks. Diet, stress, smoking and exposure to pollutants have all been associated with changes in methylation. Some studies of people conceived during periods of famine have reported differences in methylation decades later. Claims that such changes are routinely passed on across many human generations, however, deserve caution. In mammals, most epigenetic marks are erased in the germ cells and in the early embryo, and convincing evidence of inheritance over several generations comes mainly from plants and laboratory animals. Epigenetics is therefore best understood not as a rejection of genetics but as an additional layer of regulation that helps explain how a single genome can produce many different outcomes.

options: prove that epigenetic changes are always inherited for many generations

title: The Other Carbon Problem
text:
Discussions of carbon dioxide usually focus on its role in warming the planet. Yet roughly a quarter of the carbon dioxide released by human activities does not stay in the atmosphere at all; it dissolves in the oceans. This uptake has slowed climate change considerably, but it comes at a chemical cost. When carbon dioxide dissolves in seawater, it forms carbonic acid, which releases hydrogen ions and lowers the water's pH. Since the beginning of the industrial era, the average pH of surface seawater has fallen by about 0.1 units. Because the pH scale is logarithmic, this apparently small change corresponds to an increase in acidity of roughly thirty percent.

The consequences are most serious for organisms that build shells or skeletons from calcium carbonate, including corals, oysters, sea snails and some plankton. The extra hydrogen ions combine with carbonate ions, reducing the amount available for building shells. Under these conditions, organisms must spend more energy to grow, and in extreme cases existing shells may begin to dissolve. Laboratory experiments have shown deformed shells in larvae of some species, and natural sites near volcanic vents, where carbon dioxide bubbles from the seabed, offer a preview of how communities may change, with fewer calcifying species and more seaweeds.

Not every species is equally affected, and some appear surprisingly tolerant. The effects also interact with warming and with the loss of oxygen in the oceans, which makes predictions difficult. What is clear, however, is that ocean acidification cannot be solved by approaches that cool the planet without reducing carbon dioxide, such as reflecting sunlight back into space. Only lowering emissions addresses both problems at once.

explain how carbon dioxide dissolved in seawater warms the atmosphere above it

title: The Missing Mass
text:
In the 1970s, the American astronomer Vera Rubin and her colleagues measured how fast stars and gas move around the centres of spiral galaxies. According to Newton's laws, objects far from the bright centre, where most of the visible matter lies, should orbit more slowly, just as Neptune moves more slowly around the Sun than Mercury does. Instead, Rubin found that the orbital speeds remained roughly constant far into the outer regions. If only visible matter were present, these galaxies should have flown apart long ago.

The most widely accepted explanation is that galaxies are embedded in vast halos of dark matter, a form of matter that exerts gravity but neither emits nor absorbs light. Supporting evidence has since come from several independent directions: the way clusters of galaxies bend the light of more distant objects, the pattern of tiny temperature variations in the cosmic microwave background, and computer simulations showing that the large-scale structure of the universe could not have formed in the available time without additional mass. Taken together, these observations suggest that dark matter outweighs ordinary matter by a factor of about five.

What dark matter actually consists of, however, remains unknown. For decades, a leading candidate was a class of heavy particles that interact only weakly with ordinary matter, but increasingly sensitive underground detectors have so far failed to observe them. A minority of physicists argue that the problem lies not in missing matter but in our theory of gravity, which may need modification at very low accelerations. Such theories explain galaxy rotation well but struggle to account for observations of galaxy clusters. The debate illustrates how science often advances: a single unexpected measurement can expose a gap that takes generations to fill.

options: Neptune was found to move faster than Mercury, contrary to the predictions of Newton's laws
spiral galaxies were shown to contain no gas

options: The way galaxy clusters bend the light coming from more distant objects

title: The Drifting Continents
text:
In 1912, the German meteorologist Alfred Wegener proposed that the continents had once been joined in a single landmass and had slowly drifted apart. His evidence was varied and, in hindsight, persuasive. The coastlines of South America and Africa fit together like pieces of a puzzle; identical fossils of land-dwelling reptiles appeared on continents now separated by oceans; and rock formations and traces of ancient glaciers lined up when the continents were reassembled.

Most geologists nevertheless rejected the idea for several decades. Their main objection was not to Wegener's observations but to his mechanism. He suggested that continents ploughed through the ocean floor, pushed by forces related to Earth's rotation, yet physicists calculated that such forces were far too weak. Without a plausible cause, many scientists found it easier to imagine vanished land bridges that had once connected the continents. It did not help that Wegener was an outsider to geology.

The breakthrough came from the ocean floor itself. In the 1950s and 1960s, surveys revealed a vast system of underwater mountain ridges and, alongside them, symmetrical stripes of rock with alternating magnetic orientations. These stripes were explained by the idea that new crust forms at the ridges and spreads outward, recording reversals of Earth's magnetic field as it cools. Combined with the discovery that old crust sinks back into the mantle at deep ocean trenches, this led to the theory of plate tectonics. Continents, it turned out, do not plough through the seafloor; they ride on moving plates. Wegener, who died on an expedition to Greenland in 1930, did not live to see his central idea vindicated.

title: Chemicals That Refuse to Break Down
text:
Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, commonly known as PFAS, are a family of several thousand synthetic chemicals that have been produced since the 1940s. Their defining feature is the bond between carbon and fluorine, one of the strongest in organic chemistry. This bond gives PFAS remarkable properties: they repel both water and oil, withstand high temperatures and resist chemical attack. As a result, they have been used in non-stick cookware, waterproof clothing, food packaging and fire-fighting foams.

The very stability that makes PFAS so useful also makes them a problem. Because natural processes break them down extremely slowly, if at all, they have earned the nickname "forever chemicals". They have now been detected in rainwater, soil, wildlife and the blood of most people tested in industrialised countries. Some well-studied PFAS have been linked to effects on the immune system, raised cholesterol and certain cancers, which has prompted regulators to restrict them and to set increasingly strict limits for drinking water.

Removing PFAS once they are in the environment is difficult and expensive. Activated carbon filters and specialised resins can capture many of them from water, but this only transfers the chemicals to another material that must then be disposed of. Destroying them generally requires very high temperatures or energy-intensive treatments, and researchers are investigating methods that break the carbon-fluorine bond under milder conditions. Many scientists argue that, given the size of the chemical family, regulating substances one at a time is too slow. They propose treating PFAS as a single class and limiting their use to applications that are essential and for which no safer alternatives exist.

options: both the usefulness of PFAS and the fact that they persist
the low cost of fire-fighting foams
the rapid breakdown of PFAS in rainwater, soil and the bodies of wildlife
the ability of PFAS to absorb both water and oil at high temperatures
the use of PFAS as a medicine

title: The Bridge That Danced
text:
When the Tacoma Narrows Bridge opened in the state of Washington in July 1940, it was the third-longest suspension bridge in the world and a showcase of elegant, economical design. Its deck was remarkably slender: instead of a deep, open steel truss, it was stiffened by shallow solid plate girders, which made it light and graceful but also unusually flexible. Even during construction, workers noticed that the deck moved up and down in moderate winds, and the bridge soon acquired the nickname "Galloping Gertie". Drivers sometimes crossed it for the thrill of watching cars ahead disappear and reappear in the waves of the roadway.

On 7 November 1940, only four months after opening, a steady wind of roughly 65 kilometres per hour set the deck into a violent twisting motion. For about an hour, the roadway rotated back and forth until cables and supports failed and the central span collapsed into the water below. Nobody was killed, although a dog trapped in an abandoned car was lost.

The collapse is often presented in textbooks as a simple case of resonance, in which the wind pushed the bridge at its natural frequency. Engineers now regard this explanation as incomplete. A steady wind does not supply a regular periodic push in the way that a child is pushed on a swing. Instead, the twisting motion of the deck altered the airflow around it, and the airflow in turn fed energy back into the motion, a self-excited phenomenon known as aeroelastic flutter. The failure transformed bridge engineering: designers began testing models in wind tunnels and favouring deeper or aerodynamically shaped decks, practices that remain standard today.

title: Strength Through Deformation
text:
When a steel strip is passed between the rolls of a cold mill at room temperature, its thickness is reduced and its length increased, yet the most consequential change takes place at a scale invisible to the naked eye. Plastic deformation in metals proceeds through the movement of dislocations, which are line defects in the crystal lattice. As the reduction increases, new dislocations are generated in enormous numbers, whereby they become entangled with one another and obstruct each other's motion. The result, known as work hardening or strain hardening, is a marked rise in yield strength and hardness, which is accompanied by a corresponding loss of ductility.

For the producer, this phenomenon is a mixed blessing. On the one hand, it enables high-strength thin gauges to be manufactured without costly alloying additions; on the other hand, a heavily reduced strip becomes so hard and brittle that further reduction would demand excessive rolling forces and could lead to edge cracking. It is for this reason that cold-rolled coils are commonly subjected to annealing, a heat treatment during which new, strain-free grains nucleate and grow, thereby restoring the formability required for operations such as deep drawing.

Notwithstanding its apparent simplicity, the balance between hardening and annealing is a matter of considerable precision. The final properties depend not only on the total reduction but also on the annealing temperature and time, whereas a light final pass, referred to as temper rolling or skin passing, is frequently applied in order to eliminate the yield-point elongation that would otherwise produce unsightly surface markings known as Lüders bands during forming.
